blocks.x: We switched from the Monolympics to the Mono-Otanberg machine. Say something again. Your name again? Jeff Poole from Sydney, Australia.
If you'd like it to come closer to the left, then you'd better move it in a little bit.
No, no, you turned the volume up. You don't have to move.
I thought you said to move the mic closer to the left. No, if the balance of our voices are... Let's get me on the volume.
This thing.
Yeah, we're going again. Okay. Trying to do too much at once. So we were talking about the London reissues.

Yeah, that's right. Yes, well, as I said, I met Jeff Holden and a few other friends that I used to play tennis with, and I'd known some of them from around the district. The district? Around our district. Well, around our district. Oh, our district. Unfortunately, not this district. Oh, we'd be playing different music. Anyway, he invited me over to his place because I was interested in a bit of jazz, and he played me a few records, and we used to then listen to records regularly. Every second day we'd be somewhere listening to records. And we had a lot of the old reissues of the Johnny Dodds and King Olivers and the blues singers and Tommy Ladner and all that sort of stuff that they reissued. And he also had some white stuff, some of the early white, red niggles and that sort of business.
And that white New Orleans. Oh, well, he had bits and pieces, yeah.

I think he had the Popper Lane record, you know, the Popper Lane's children record and a few of those things. And we used to just sort of collect records. One of the first records I ever got was, and I remember when I got it I thought it was the only copy in existence in the world. I got a Bix record. And I'd read, you know, we used to read a little bit of books and that and then, and there's, you know, all these glorious mysteries that shroud characters like Bix because he was a big hard drinker and died young and all this sort of business. And I got this Bix record and I thought it was the end of the earth, you know. But we used to listen to those records and we also got some George Lewis records, which were just coming out then. Those, also on London, you know, a couple of LPs with Alvin Alcorn and the Quartech on the other side. Mm-hmm. And, and Jazz Aphespas. Now this was all sort of, this was purely in a small clique of our own, if you like to call it a clique. And it was completely oblivious to any jazz scene that was in Sydney. And I didn't even know it existed, but Geoff Halton knew of the Sydney Jazz Club. He'd been there once or twice. So we then decided to go down there. So we went to the Sydney Jazz Club and we, I was quite amazed to see a mob of fellows up on the stage playing this stuff, or a semblance of this stuff. Mm-hmm. I mean, though, at that stage of the game, that's about 19, about 1959. Oh, they weren't young men, there's the fellows in the Paramount Jazz Band and they were in their thirties then. And they were playing this sort of stuff. And I was quite amazed to see these fellows actually up there playing the instruments and doing this sort of thing. What do you mean by this sort of thing, like...? Playing jazz, like, like, I happened to learn I had associated purely with these records.
You mean, were they playing like Dix or Latin Air?

Well, no, they were just playing, you know, assemblance of jazz. They were playing sort of this sort of music. And, you know, I'd never heard it live before, I'm sure. I'd never heard that sort of thing. And so I was quite sort of intrigued with it. I remember the first night I went there, because I was, at that stage, I was very green to this sort of music. And Jeff Holden and a couple of the others have been listening to jazz records for a few months at that stage, possibly a year or so. And they knew a few of the tunes. And I can remember going along and they'd sort of, they used to have me on that member, saying, what's the name of this one, you know? And I'd say, I don't know. And they'd say, it's so-and-so. Is it? Yeah, you know, it's on that record. So-and-so and so-and-so. And I thought, this would be how they used to think they were the world's authority on jazz. Anyway, we then sort of used to go to the jazz club every week. We sort of, you know, I didn't have any other particular interest. I wasn't interested in rock and roll or anything like that. And I certainly wasn't interested in the bodgie crowd that used to be prevalent at that stage of the game. The what crowd?
Yeah, the bodgies, you know, don't you have bodgies here? And we don't have that term. Well, it's, you know, sort of, leather-jacketed, motorbike, rock and roll. Rockers. Oh, yeah.
You call them rockers?

Well, I know what you mean. Yeah. Well, I don't know what you call them. Like mods and rockers in England. Yeah, yeah, that sort of thing. With that equivalent of that. Well, this is, this is, this is a lot of the younger kids at that stage got on this kick when the Bill Haley records came out, you know, the rockers.

And we weren't interested in that at all. I wasn't. So we used to go to the jazz club every Saturday night from then on and listen and so on and so. And, as I say, I'd, I'd, I'd played the bugle. Mm-hmm. And I, I'd, just around about, just before that stage, I'd, I'd managed to bully my mother into buying me a trumpet. Mm-hmm. Which I was going to learn to play and I had a few lessons on, on, on the trumpet just to sort of, you know, I started off having lessons. I didn't know I was going to stop having lessons. I started off having lessons and they always teach the fingerings and all this stuff first. Anyway, and then we started getting some jazz. And one of the other fellas who was in the, in the crowd with us, uh, Bob Conry, he, he, he'd been listening for a while too and he was, uh, he was mad on George. And, uh, he'd bought himself a clarinet and he wanted to learn to play the clarinet and he just happened to mention one night, he said, oh, you know, I've got a clarinet. And I said, well, I've got a trumpet. And at that stage of the game, we'd never even sort of entertained the idea of actually playing this music, you know. I said, oh, well, I've got a trumpet. And he said, oh, I've got a clarinet. And then Jeff Holden didn't play anything so he got a washboard, obviously. Mm-hmm. And then we used to, uh, just get together and, and when we'd play records, we'd occasionally have a bit of a fiddle around and, uh, and we sort of, uh, bought, I can remember we went out and bought a book full of, you know, these, uh, books of Dixieland tunes. Mm-hmm. They have them over there, sort of, Dixie, stock Dixieland arrangements, you know, and they had things like, I remember one of them was Wolverine Blues. And we learnt Wolverine Blues, we thought, which was, uh, the, the, the first bit of the chorus, which goes, da, da, da, you know, that bit. We could play those three notes, uh, but after that, it got difficult, we had to stop, go back and start again. But anyway, we got sort of, uh, we got started off in, in that way. Now, this was, this is all, um, Can I stop you?

Yeah. You said the clarinet player like George, who is George? I'm assuming George Lewis. Uh, well, yeah, that's correct. Yeah. Yeah. Well, I'm sorry, I used that term in a too familiar way. Yeah. Well, naturally you would, but I, you know, I just want to make it clear.
Yeah. Well, getting back to what I was about to say, I'm, I'm sort of…
No, no. I still, I have to interrupt you again on another point. What was the jazz club like in Australia? You know, they're different here.

Uh-huh. Yeah, well, the jazz club in Sydney, um, well, it, it started out as, um, so I imagine, as a group of fellows who used to play instruments and got together, and they started, uh, they hired a, a cheap hall in town and they used to play it for Saturday night just for their own enjoyment and then they opened the doors to see if people would come in. Well, um, um, when I first started going down there, they didn't get very many people, they used to get 50 or 100 people a night, on a Saturday night. Um, and that's what it was, it was just like a, really a dance where a jazz band played. But you could become a member of the club and then you'd get, they'd send you the quarterly rag, which is their magazine, you have, I suppose you've had it here, haven't you? No, I don't think I've ever seen it. Well, we'll talk about that afterwards and I'll arrange to have it sent to you every month, every quarter. Um, and you could be a member of the club and then you got in for a couple of bob less next week sort of thing and then they, they used to have record, uh, rhythm club meetings, they call them in those days. This is before my time, I've only heard about this by word of mouth, I've never been to them. They used to have record nights and so and so would have a good record collection and, uh, um, then they'd have a night where all the people would go to his place and they, they used to play. Um, I remember Fred Starkey used to have his, uh, his treasured Jabbo Smiths. You know the Jabbo Smiths rhythm aces things? Yeah. And, uh, they were, they were sort of treasured pieces and you'd go along and, uh, if you became really familiar he'd play you his Jabbo Smith rhythm aces. Anyway, that was before my time. Um, but that's what the jazz club's like, really and still is, a Saturday night dance which has a jazz band playing. That's all. And, uh, consequently you, you get a crowd of, uh, um, well a small percentage of the crowd these days are jazz fans. The rest of them are kids who, uh, like dancing to jazz and like to sort of, you know.
Mm-hmm.

But, uh, getting back to, uh, the background, um, I wanted to make a point of, uh, of this for a particular reason. It'll come out later. At this stage of the game, this is getting back to our small group in Coogee and Bondi, that's where Jeff Holden left. Um, we started to play and we listened to records and we listened to these George Lewis records, uh, which came out. And we just sort of took them as, as also being jazz records, obviously. But, uh, there was definitely a difference to the sound in those and the sound of the, uh, of the early reissue records. I remember when, when we first bought Jazz at Vespers, we used to play it over and over again, over and over again, Jazz at Vespers. And, uh, anyway, I developed, uh, or we all developed, a sort of, uh, preference for that stuff, um, to the, um, to, well, to the white stuff. Almost immediately. It was a very little time, I think, that, uh, it was a very short time when I, when I ever listened much, with much interest, or, or with much admiration to the early white bands. Especially the Rett Nichols and that sort of business. I mean, uh, I think it's, uh, it's, well, it was to me pretty obvious straight away that there was not much depth in that. And, uh, anyway, we started to, uh, we kept on playing and fiddling around. And we went to the Jazz Club one week, and we used to be there so often that, uh, they sort of got to know us. And they knew that we liked jazz, because we, um, then started to ask for a few tunes, and ask them so-and-so, how do they like this musician and that musician? And they obviously knew that we were interested in jazz and collected records and things like this. And so one fellow came up to us and said, you know, do you play instruments? And we sort of said, well, yeah, yeah, we do, sort of a little bit. And they said, well, uh, and they had this, every second Friday night, they used to hire a little, a little old Ramshackle Hall, which, uh, uh, which would really fit well in New Orleans, I've always imagined. Because it was one of those old wooden, um, and it was called the Forester's Hall, which was like a lodge. It was a Forester's Lodge Hall, and they used to get that, I think, for 10 shillings on, on, on every second Friday night. And all the musicians, um, the jazz musicians in Sydney, when I say all, there was a sort of a clique of them. There were two bands that played at the Sydney Jazz Club, plus other various musicians, used to come along to this hall and just have a, uh, a jam session, and then, and play a few numbers and drink a few bottles and things like this. And this fellow said, well, why don't you come out to the Forester's? You know, we have a, a jazz school out there. And, uh, uh, you can come out there and the other musicians will teach you to play. And so we thought this was, uh, you know, just the, just the ants' pants. So the night came around and out we went, myself and the clarinet player, Bob Conry. And, uh, I had a, uh, at that stage of the game, I'd, I'd got rid of my gold trumpet. I realised then that the only thing to do was to play a little, lull, battered cornet. Or I thought, anyway, I don't know, I had a cornet, which was a horrible, atrocious instrument, you know. But it looked good, I thought. So I had a cornet and he had his clarinet and we went up to this hall, where we were supposed to be, have a lesson, and have someone teach us. So I arrived and I'm sitting around and the fellow said, oh, well, right, you're gonna, you're gonna play now? And we sort of said, well, what do you mean play? He said, well, we organised a group for you to play in. And so we were stuck up on the, on the stage to play. Well, it wasn't the stage, it was just on the floor level in the corner. Stuck up to play with this group. And I sort of said, boy, no. At that stage of the game, I only knew two tunes. I knew, uh, I'll record cross because I'd listened to the George record so often and learnt the tune. And I knew the first half of Down by the Riverside. I didn't know the chorus of Down by the Riverside. So one fellow had to, one of the other trumpet players had to quickly teach me how the second part went. And then we played two tunes, my entire repertoire at that time. And, uh, so we played the two tunes and, you know, I don't remember what it was like. You can imagine the first time you've ever played in a group and there was a whole rhythm section and everything. And I, you know, we played them. And apparently, yeah, of course I just played the tune over and over again, straight, sort of, uh, just played the melody. There was no such thing as an improvisation at that stage for me. And, uh, so-
Can I entirely change the subject?
Hmm?

Can I entirely change the subject? Because I want to bring up something which is in a state of change for you right now. We're about halfway through the tape. We'll stop at your first public performance and then take that up later. Uh, what do you think of New Orleans today, your impression after having been here for how long? Have you been here?
I've been here since last, uh, um, last Wednesday night I arrived. So I've been here about a week.
About a, well, yeah. Well this is, uh, Wednesday in the afternoon. Yeah.
Oh, this is Thursday.
I mean Thursday, well. So it's a weekend. Yeah. Just over a week. Uh, so why don't you tell me a little bit about that and we'll let that develop.

Yeah, well, uh, my impressions are sort of, obviously, they're different to what I had because, you know, you build up a sort of, uh, you build up a, probably a glorified impression of these things. You must. From reading books and magazines and, and New Orleans to me, uh, well the city is, uh, is more modern than I wanted it to be, if you can understand what I mean. Uh-huh. I wanted New Orleans to be, I think, now that, I mean I've realised now that it was ridiculous, but I think I wanted New Orleans to be what it probably was like in the twenties or thirties. Uh, a, a, a little, a quaint French village or something like this, where they had a French quarter and all this business. Uh, you want to see these great big sprawling lights and big roads and, and over expressways and all this sort of stuff. Um, then I got to New Orleans Airport. And I, I mean, I've been wanting to come here for years and I've been wondering what would we like to come here for years and I've read stories about fellas who've come here and I read one story in the Eureka magazine about a fella who drove down and he was in the bus for two and a half days, but as soon as he, he got to New Orleans and drove down the beautiful streets with the trees down the centre, he's, he came to life or some rubbish like that. And I probably thought I might do something like this, but I didn't know that the New Orleans Airport and, uh, all I wanted to do was get the preservation hall cause it was getting late and I wanted to hear the band that night. Uh, but yeah, it sort of, it did shatter my image a bit because the place does seem awfully sort of, uh, uh, mind you, this is the first American city I've ever been in. Mm-hmm. Stopped in, I didn't stop in Washington or Atlanta and it seemed very loud and garish to me and all sorts of big cars and wide streets and, and lots of neon signs. Anyway, I, uh, got rid of my bags and went to preservation hall and, uh, well, I, I walked around the corner and heard Jim, you know. And that to me was something because Jim, Jim, it's, it's always been a dream of mine to, to listen to Jim Robinson, you know. And as soon as I heard the trombone I knew it was Jim and I thought possibly Endless Band and it was Endless Band, you know. But, um, well I don't know, I don't know what I should say about, uh, my impressions of the situation.
Well go ahead and we can restrict it until, you know.
We'll do so, you know.
Yeah, okay, go ahead.
This is restricted.
Right. Until some future time, upon your decision as to when it should be restricted. Okay, go ahead.

Well to me the whole set up in, in, in preservation hall is, uh, uh, it's a little bit, uh, a little bit confusing, a bit strange, a bit sick. This business of, uh, of having a bloke, uh, front a band which he doesn't pick and things like this, uh, just isn't, doesn't seem right to me. Uh, anyway I might threaten people's toes there. Uh, musically, I've been very impressed with a lot, and very unimpressed with a lot. Uh, cause I, I mean, I didn't, I don't think I expected everyone here to be good. I'm sure I didn't, you know, and it's, it's getting late in the era of, of the old negro players anyway, and a lot of the best ones have gone, you know. Uh, but there are a lot of musicians who've really impressed me. I had a good, a very good start as far as I was concerned by, uh, first of all having Elton Purnell come out to Australia, whom I regard as, as, as, as, as the best piano player, best jazz piano player, you know, on record. He's my favourite, I prefer him to Jelly Roll more than. And, uh, we had him out, and, and, uh, there was certainly no disappointment there. And then when I got to England, I heard John Handy, it knocked me right out. Completely floored me, here John Handy, because he's just, he's just, uh, absolutely genius, you know. He's such a hot, fiery player, and, and he's so good on his instrument and everything, you know, that, uh, it knocked me right out. And I thought, well, you know, uh, if everyone in New Orleans is as good as that, then, uh, uh, I won't be disappointed. Well, obviously everyone in New Orleans isn't as good as that. And I haven't heard many that I think are as good as that. Uh, there are a few that are, that are as good, I think, but not many. Uh, and this is another point, getting back to it, that, that, that, that, that, that completely bewilders me. The fact that, um, a fellow like John Handy isn't used Preservation Hall because he plays the saxophone. Now this, this is just, you know, well, we'll leave it at that because it might get to the years of, uh.
No, we can restrict anything you want us to, speak your mind. Well, I mean, you know, you know what I mean, you know.

I know exactly what you mean. The fact that they'll use clarinet players like, now, uh, um, not taking anything against him, because I quite like his playing, and he did play some nice things, but the fact that they'll use a clarinet player like Polo Barnes in Preservation Hall, and not use a saxophone player like John Handy, to me, is rubbish, because John Handy is, is, is just so much better, that it isn't funny. The fact that they'll use Harry Shields, and not John Handy, is, is ridiculous, because Harry Shields is quite a nice clarinet player, but he's just nothing compared to John Handy as a New Orleans musician. I mean, you know, this, this is the thing that, that gets me, that a place like that can be so basically misinformed. I mean, Preservation Hall is, is now the sort of, the home of New Orleans jazz, you know, almost in this city, isn't it? Well, not the home of New Orleans jazz, but it's, it's the place where, um, all the best and most authentic musicians play. Who said that?
Well, it seems to be.
It seems to be to me. Where else? Dixieland Hall. Dixieland Hall just seems to be one. What about the brass bands?
Well, I mean, I'm talking about, in, in, in dance bands now.

I'm not talking about street bands. Well, I mean, I'm talking about, in, in dance bands now. I'm not talking about street bands. Well, I think people's homes, you have to consider that, private parties. Yeah, yeah.
Well, I'm, I'm talking about somewhere where it's regularly. You mean a publicly known tourist place? No, where it's regularly available. Yeah, well, that's, it's probably the best place in town.
Yeah. It's generally accepted at such a moment.
But, but the, the, the, the, the basic thing, what I'm getting back to it is, how can that place, if it does that, how can that place have a piano with broken strings on it and
so much out of tune that it doesn't matter? I mean, I don't think that's a good thing.
Well, I'm talking about, I'm talking about, I'm talking about, I'm talking about, but, but, but, but the, the, the, the basic thing, what I'm getting back to it is, how

can that place, if it does that, how can that place have a piano with broken strings on it and so much out of tune that it doesn't matter? I mean, if he can't afford a few dollars to fix up that piano or buy a brand new piano, then nobody can. Well, maybe he's not making enough money then.
Oh, yeah.

I've been there every night I've been here and the basket that goes out through the back door is, they could buy a piano every night. I mean, you know, they're, they're not losing anything. And, and this, that sort of thing for one, that, that, that, they, they don't have a good piano for the musicians to play on, it's just absolutely ridiculous. And then this business of picking blokes to play there is, it's equally ridiculous. When you put fellas with someone else, just because, um, he's well liked around there. And the, the other point of, of refusing to hire musicians and threatening them, if you play in so and so place, you don't play here again. That to me is just stupid. Preservation Hall, as far as I, uh, always understood, was originally created by Ken Middles, wasn't it? Yeah, he's the one who started it. Was started as a place for the good of the musicians, to give them somewhere to play and, and, and for the good of New Orleans music, for everyone to listen to around the world. And this, that, that, that has done this, because as a result of them playing there regularly and things, a lot of records have been made and a lot of good has been done. But, um, I can't see that it's doing the musicians any good if they're only allowed to play there on the nights when they're hired to play there anyway. And then, and they're threatened with the expulsion if they play otherwise. Well, look at Raymond Burke. Now, Raymond Burke's one of the best players down here now, isn't he?
That's what a lot of people say. I haven't heard.

Well, I haven't heard Raymond Burke in person. I've heard him on records. Yeah. And, and he's, he's, from, from what I hear from people who've been here, he's one of the best clarinet players down here now.
Mm-hm.
Now, he, he's been expelled from the Hall because he worked across the road.
Mm-hm.

I mean, that, that to me is, the, the fact that people can stand over my, I mean, my idols, if you like to call them that. Mm-hm. I mean, not so much Raymond Burke. The fact that people can tell Jim Robinson and George Lewis and those fellows where they're allowed to or not allowed to play or they're expelled from, from playing at Preservation Hall. And the fact that those same blokes do rely on that place for a living is, to me, a little bit sick. So, in general, my impressions of, of the situation, the way it stands in, in, in the city and, and with Preservation Hall, is a bit of a, a let down, mm-hm, from that point of view. And, er, and see, see, obviously the people who are, are popular, er, with Jaffe, are the ones that Jaffe hires every night. And also, as far as I can see, er, it, it, it's fast turning into a, a, a place where, er, they want to guarantee they make their big money. And the people that make big money, the people who've got, er, er, as that, bloody idiot artist, if you don't mind me swearing on your tape. No, see, I don't want to. She can always shut her ears. The people who have an image, like Sweet Emma, for instance, because she's had a lot of publicity and because she's a little, old, rickety old woman that people like to look at and say, isn't that amazing that a little, old woman like that can play the piano? The people I hear who draw people, he uses regularly, more regularly than other musicians who are better, just so that he's going to get a good crowd, as far as I can see.
You object to the commercialism of the place, is what you're saying, you know?

At the expense of, er, of, of some other musicians, I do, yes. Yeah. I do. I, I object to the fact that some musicians who, er, who are going to draw a crowd are used more than others because they're going to draw a crowd. This, to me, isn't giving equal advantage to New Orleans musicians, which the place, I thought, was supposed to do. Especially when, er, superior musicians are not used there because they don't play an instrument that's acceptable or they, or they haven't got a name that's shrouded in mystery or something. Or a leg shrouded in bells.
Well then, your impression of the place was that it was a non-commercial place designed to, to help New Orleans, musicians in general, not any one particular group or anything.

My impression was that it was, had started out as a non-commercial place to allow these musicians to, er, to keep in practice and keep playing and make money and make a living because most of them are too old to make a living otherwise. And my impression was that it had developed because of its authenticity and because of some mere stroke of luck, it had developed into a successful commercial venture. But I didn't think that it was being run as a commercial venture. I thought that it was a commercial venture in spite of itself. And I'm most disappointed to see that it isn't. And this fact of musicians not being used there because someone down there doesn't like the fellow, or they've had an argument with him, or he doesn't play the right sort of instrument, or he's played across the road at so-and-so's hamburger shop or something like that, that to me is completely bewildering because as far as I'm concerned, if it's a place that is designed to keep alive New Orleans Jazz, the musicianship of the player and the fact that he can play his music and how well he can play it should determine whether or not he works it, whether he's worked over the road, whether he's worked anywhere or whether he plays saxophone or a slide banana.
What about tunes? What sort of tunes do they play there?

Very restricted tunes in a lot of cases. I mean, this I don't mind so much. I don't mind Sweet Emma playing Closer Walk three times a night because I like to hear her sing it every time. But they do play fairly restricted tunes. They play Bill Bailey every night without fail at least once, often twice. They have to play The Saints. Well, I mean, they do sort of in a way have to, and I can understand that because I've had to play The Saints myself when I didn't want to. The bands that play don't really disappoint me. Some musicians in the bands do, and there are other musicians in the city that are better, that aren't used there, and I wish were used there. It's not so much the music that disappoints me as the administration. You know, the situation as it stands with the place and the way it's run. To me, that's a big disappointment.
Who are some of the musicians who've really impressed you there? The musicians that really impressed me are Jim, especially Jim.

George, of course, Lewis Nelson, Chester Zardes, one of the most of all, possibly because I didn't expect to see him and because he just plays excellent bass. Soi, Sammy Penn, Manuel Paul very, very much. I think Manuel Paul is one of the best players I've heard here. Thomas. Kid Thomas. Kid Thomas. I like Frank Miliere. I quite like Sweet Emma's playing. Joe Butler is a good singer and quite a good bass player. I wouldn't say he's excellent. I like drag, the night drag played. Alec Bigard, he has impressed me at times. As you know, he tends to be a little bit unsteady at times. Who else now? That's about all, so far. Except John Handy, of course. Where else have you been? I've been to England.
No, in New Orleans. Oh, wait a minute.
This reminds me, Albert Pertman impressed me quite well. I was very unimpressed. Better not say who I was unimpressed with. Better not.
But, uh... I can restrict it.
Well, I was surprisingly unimpressed with Frog Joseph for one.
You've been to some other places?
I've been to Dixieland Hall. And, uh... I've been to the Red Garter. I went to the Red Garter when Jack...
We're running out of tape.
I'm running out of time, so we'll have to call it to a halt now.
And we'll do it more later. Okay.
